reason: The provided sources contain ample verified facts to support a compelling 45-second script about the Peshtigo Fire.
story: On the night of October 8, 1871, a booming Wisconsin lumber town called Peshtigo vanished in less than two hours. Following a severe summer drought and rampant land-clearing slash fires, an eastward-moving cold front brought hurricane-force winds that turned small fires into a monstrous firestorm. Generating temperatures of 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit and fierce updrafts, the blaze vaporized entire forests and caused buildings to literally explode. Hundreds of desperate residents plunged into the frigid Peshtigo River to escape the wall of flame, while others succumbed to smoke, drowning, or hypothermia. Between 1,200 and 2,500 people lost their lives, making it the deadliest wildfire in American history. Yet because the Great Chicago Fire erupted four hundred miles south on that exact same night, the apocalyptic inferno at Peshtigo was cast into historical shadow and largely forgotten.
angle: It is the deadliest wildfire in American history, killing up to 2,500 people—at least five times the death toll of the Great Chicago Fire—yet it was almost entirely forgotten because it happened on the exact same night.

claims.claim: The Peshtigo Fire occurred on October 8, 1871.
Peshtigo, Wisconsin had a pre-fire population of approximately 1,700 to 2,000 residents.
The fire burned approximately 1.2 million acres of land.
The Peshtigo Fire is the deadliest wildfire in recorded American history.
The death toll is estimated between 1,500 and 2,500 people.
The Great Chicago Fire occurred on the exact same night, killing roughly 300 people and overshadowing Peshtigo in the national press.
An eastward-moving cold front and pressure gradient created strong winds that merged slash-and-burn land management fires.
The firestorm reached temperatures of at least 2,000 degrees Fahrenheit and wind speeds of 110 miles per hour.
Many citizens sought refuge by immersing themselves in the Peshtigo River, where some tragically drowned or succumbed to hypothermia.
An accurate death toll has never been definitively determined because all local records and many victims were completely reduced to ash.
Father Peter Pernin was a Catholic priest who survived the disaster by entering the river and later published a detailed eyewitness account.
In Door County, the community of Williamsonville was struck by a fire whirl, leaving only a handful of survivors from its residents.

disputed: The exact death toll varies between estimates of 1,200 and 2,500 due to destroyed local records; scripts should attribute this as a range according to historical estimates.

A long-running speculation suggests the fires were ignited by fragments of Biela's Comet, but modern science and experts dispute this as unproven legend or hypothesis; scripts should present it only as speculation or leave it out.
